name: MADAGASCAR

flag.title: Madagascar
flag.note: White & red vertical, then red over green

lead: Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island — a floating ark in the Indian Ocean. Drifted from Africa 170 million years ago, about 90% of its animals live nowhere else on Earth. Over 100 lemur species, half the world's chameleons, and enormous ancient baobabs call it home. Scientists nickname it the eighth continent.
geo: Madagascar sits 400 km off Africa's east coast. A highland spine runs the island's length, dropping to a rainforest east coast. The west is drier, lined with giant baobabs and razor-sharp limestone towers called tsingy — 'where you cannot walk barefoot' in Malagasy.

The south is near-desert, full of spiny plants found nowhere else. Six climate zones pack into one island. Red-clay soil gives Madagascar its nickname: the Great Red Island. Humpback whales breed in the warm offshore waters each winter.
animals: Over 100 lemur species live here, from the 30-gram mouse lemur — the world's tiniest primate — to the indri, whose haunting wail echoes for kilometres. About 90% of Madagascar's wildlife is endemic, meaning it exists absolutely nowhere else on the planet.

The fossa, Madagascar's top predator, looks like a small puma but is related to the mongoose. Half the world's chameleons live here, including the Brookesia micra — barely thumbnail-sized. Panther chameleons flash electric colours, and frogs glow under ultraviolet light.
culture: Malagasy culture revolves around ancestors called razana, believed to watch over the living. Families follow fady — personal taboos passed down for generations. The most striking tradition is famadihana: families exhume ancestors' bones, wrap them in fresh silk, then dance with them joyfully before reburial.

Rice is sacred — Malagasy eat it three times a day and have over 30 words for rice dishes. The national dish, romazava, is a brothy zebu-beef stew with wild greens. Zebu cattle appear in every ceremony. Village celebrations fill with hira gasy music and costumed storytelling.
history: Polynesian sailors crossed 6,000 km of open ocean to settle Madagascar around 2,000 years ago — one of history's boldest voyages. Bantu farmers arrived from Africa later. By the 1700s the Merina kingdom had united much of the island under a highland royal family.

France colonised Madagascar in 1896, exiling the queen and ending the monarchy. A brutal 1947 uprising killed tens of thousands. On 26 June 1960 Madagascar gained full independence, a date still marked as a national holiday with parades across the island.
wows: Madagascar grows about 80% of all the world's vanilla, yet it is one of the planet's poorest countries.
The first Malagasy settlers sailed from Indonesia — over 6,000 km away — not from nearby Africa.
Madagascar hosts nearly half of all chameleon species on Earth: about 59 found nowhere else.
Tsingy limestone spires are razor-sharp; wildlife shelters inside, safe from human hunters.
Malagasy is an Austronesian language, more closely related to Malay than to Swahili.
No zoo has ever kept an indri lemur alive long-term; it refuses to survive in captivity.
Each family has unique fady: one may never eat eel; another may never face north at meals.

myths.fact: Its people and language trace to Indonesia, 6,000 km east. Malagasy is Austronesian. The island split from Africa 170 million years ago — long before humans appeared.
Lemurs are prosimians — a far older primate branch. They evolved alone on Madagascar for millions of years, entirely separate from monkeys or apes.
